knowledge_points.description: Define an AI search problem using states, initial state, actions, transition model, goal test, and path cost.
learning_objectives: Identify the components of a search problem.
Explain how a real task can be converted into a state-space search problem.
common_misconceptions: Thinking that the search algorithm itself defines the problem.
Ignoring the path cost when formulating the problem.
mastery_criteria: Can define state, action, goal test, and path cost for a simple problem.

knowledge_points.description: Understand how states and operators define the possible transitions in a search problem.
learning_objectives: Describe what a state space is.
Explain how operators generate successor states.
common_misconceptions: Confusing a state with a node in the search tree.
Assuming all state spaces are finite and small.
mastery_criteria: Can list valid successors for a given state.

knowledge_points.description: Compare tree search and graph search, especially how repeated states are handled.
learning_objectives: Explain why repeated states can cause inefficiency or loops.
Distinguish search tree nodes from problem states.
common_misconceptions: Assuming tree search and graph search always expand the same nodes.
Believing that repeated-state checking is only an optimization.
mastery_criteria: Can explain the role of an explored set in graph search.

knowledge_points.title_zh: 边界队列与已探索集合
knowledge_points.description: Understand the frontier as the set of generated but unexpanded nodes, and the explored set as visited states.
learning_objectives: Describe the role of the frontier.
Explain why different data structures lead to different search strategies.
common_misconceptions: Confusing frontier with explored set.
Thinking the frontier is always a queue.
mastery_criteria: Can trace how the frontier changes during BFS or DFS.

knowledge_points.description: Breadth-first search expands the shallowest nodes first, typically using a FIFO queue.
learning_objectives: Trace the expansion order of BFS.
Explain when BFS is complete and optimal.
common_misconceptions: Thinking BFS is always optimal even when step costs differ.
Confusing shallowest solution with lowest-cost solution.
mastery_criteria: Can explain why BFS finds the shortest path in number of steps when all step costs are equal.

knowledge_points.description: Depth-first search expands the deepest node first, typically using a stack or recursion.
learning_objectives: Trace the expansion order of DFS.
Explain why DFS may fail in infinite-depth spaces.
common_misconceptions: Thinking DFS always finds the shortest path.
Thinking DFS and backtracking are exactly the same concept.
mastery_criteria: Can provide a counterexample where DFS finds a non-shortest solution.

knowledge_points.title_zh: 完备性、最优性与复杂度
knowledge_points.description: Evaluate search algorithms using completeness, optimality, time complexity, and space complexity.
learning_objectives: Define completeness and optimality.
Compare search algorithms using standard evaluation criteria.
common_misconceptions: Confusing completeness with optimality.
Thinking a faster algorithm is always a better algorithm.
mastery_criteria: Can compare BFS and DFS in terms of completeness, optimality, time, and space.

knowledge_points.description: Uniform-cost search expands the node with the lowest path cost and is optimal under nonnegative step costs.
learning_objectives: Explain the difference between BFS and UCS.
Trace UCS using path costs.
common_misconceptions: Thinking UCS and BFS are always identical.
Confusing path cost with depth.
mastery_criteria: Can determine which node UCS expands next based on cumulative path cost.

knowledge_points.title_zh: 有信息搜索与启发函数
knowledge_points.description: Understand how heuristic functions estimate distance or cost to the goal and guide search.
learning_objectives: Define a heuristic function.
Explain why heuristics can improve search efficiency.
common_misconceptions: Thinking a heuristic must always be exact.
Ignoring the difference between estimated cost and true cost.
mastery_criteria: Can propose a simple heuristic for a grid-world search problem.

knowledge_points.description: Greedy best-first search expands the node that appears closest to the goal according to the heuristic value.
learning_objectives: Explain how greedy best-first search selects nodes.
Identify why greedy search is not guaranteed to be optimal.
common_misconceptions: Thinking the locally best heuristic choice always gives the best path.
Confusing greedy best-first search with A* search.
mastery_criteria: Can construct or explain a case where greedy search gives a suboptimal solution.

knowledge_points.description: A* search evaluates nodes using f(n) = g(n) + h(n), combining path cost and heuristic estimate.
learning_objectives: Explain the meaning of g(n), h(n), and f(n).
Trace the node selection process of A*.
common_misconceptions: Thinking A* only uses the heuristic.
Confusing A* with greedy best-first search.
mastery_criteria: Can calculate f(n) values and choose the next node to expand.

knowledge_points.description: Understand the conditions under which heuristics allow A* to guarantee optimality.
learning_objectives: Define admissibility.
Define consistency.
Explain how these properties relate to A* optimality.
common_misconceptions: Thinking every heuristic guarantees optimality.
Confusing admissibility with consistency.
mastery_criteria: Can judge whether a simple heuristic is admissible or consistent in a small graph.

knowledge_points.description: A course-unit topic covering search that operates from candidate states rather than retaining a full search tree.
learning_objectives: Recognize local search as a Search Algorithms unit topic.
Relate a local-search question to the course material source.
common_misconceptions: Assuming every search method must retain a full path tree.
Treating a local-search source as a replacement for graph-search definitions.
mastery_criteria: Can identify when a question concerns local search.

knowledge_points.description: A local-search method that repeatedly moves from the current state to a better neighboring state and stops when no better neighbor is available.
learning_objectives: Describe the neighbor-improvement rule used by hill climbing.
Recognize its local-optimum limitation and the role of randomization variants.
common_misconceptions: Thinking hill climbing retains every path from the initial state.
Assuming a locally better neighbor guarantees a global optimum.
mastery_criteria: Can trace a hill-climbing move using a stated evaluation function.

knowledge_points.description: A local-search method that combines improvement moves with controlled randomness, using a temperature schedule to reduce randomness over time.
learning_objectives: Explain why simulated annealing may accept a non-improving move.
Describe the role of a temperature schedule.
common_misconceptions: Thinking simulated annealing is an unrestricted random walk.
Assuming its randomness remains constant throughout search.
mastery_criteria: Can distinguish the early and late roles of randomness in simulated annealing.

knowledge_points.description: A population-based search approach that iterates selection, recombination, and mutation, with fitter individuals more likely to produce descendants.
learning_objectives: Identify population, fitness, selection, recombination, and mutation.
Explain how these operations create later generations.
common_misconceptions: Thinking evolutionary search follows a single candidate path.
Confusing a fitness value with a guaranteed optimal solution.
mastery_criteria: Can explain the role of selection and mutation in a simple evolutionary-search cycle.

knowledge_points.title_zh: 迭代加深深度优先搜索
knowledge_points.description: Repeatedly run depth-limited depth-first search with increasing depth limits.
learning_objectives: Explain how iterative deepening raises its depth limit.
Compare its repeated shallow-node generation with BFS and DFS trade-offs.
common_misconceptions: Thinking iterative deepening expands every node only once.
Assuming it is optimal when action costs are unequal.
mastery_criteria: Can explain why iterative deepening is complete and when its shallowest solution is optimal.

knowledge_points.title_zh: LLM 搜索与测试时扩展
knowledge_points.description: A course-unit topic on search in the context of large language models and test-time computation.
learning_objectives: Recognize LLM search and test-time scaling as a course topic.
Locate the corresponding course-material source for a question.
common_misconceptions: Assuming LLM search automatically changes learner mastery.
Treating test-time scaling as a replacement for course-grounded evidence.
mastery_criteria: Can identify when a question concerns LLM search or test-time scaling.

knowledge_points.description: A course-unit topic about search in settings with opposing decision makers.
learning_objectives: Recognize adversarial search as a Search Algorithms unit topic.
Locate the corresponding course-material source for a question.
common_misconceptions: Assuming all search problems have only one decision maker.
Treating adversarial-search material as ordinary shortest-path search.
mastery_criteria: Can identify when a question concerns adversarial search.

knowledge_points.description: A deterministic game-search method that selects actions by alternating MAX and MIN values in a two-player zero-sum game tree.
learning_objectives: Identify MAX and MIN decision nodes.
Explain how terminal utilities are propagated through a game tree.
common_misconceptions: Treating every game-tree node as controlled by the same player.
Choosing the locally largest value at a MIN node.
mastery_criteria: Can compute the minimax value of a small fully specified game tree.

knowledge_points.description: A minimax optimization that maintains alpha and beta bounds and prunes successors that cannot affect the ancestor decision.
learning_objectives: Explain the alpha and beta bounds.
Recognize when an alpha-beta cutoff occurs.
common_misconceptions: Thinking pruning changes the minimax decision.
Assuming search order has no effect on pruning efficiency.
mastery_criteria: Can identify a pruned branch in a small alpha-beta trace.

knowledge_points.description: A resource-limited game-search technique that estimates nonterminal state quality from weighted features when exhaustive search to terminal states is impractical.
learning_objectives: Explain why a nonterminal evaluation function is needed under limited search depth.
Identify weighted state features as an evaluation design approach.
common_misconceptions: Treating an evaluation value as a terminal utility.
Assuming alpha-beta alone makes deep exhaustive game search feasible.
mastery_criteria: Can explain how a feature-based evaluation supports depth-limited game search.

knowledge_points.description: A search approach that estimates a state's value through repeated randomized simulations and their observed outcomes.
learning_objectives: Explain how repeated simulations estimate a state value.
Relate win-rate estimates to simulated outcomes.
common_misconceptions: Treating one simulation as a reliable state evaluation.
Assuming simulation budgets are unlimited.
mastery_criteria: Can explain how sampled outcomes form a win-rate estimate.

knowledge_points.description: The trade-off between trying uncertain choices to improve estimates and selecting choices with the best currently known reward.
learning_objectives: Distinguish exploration from exploitation.
Explain why either extreme can be inadequate under a limited budget.
common_misconceptions: Thinking exploitation produces a trustworthy estimate after one trial.
Thinking exploration never uses reward information.
mastery_criteria: Can describe the exploration-exploitation trade-off in a multi-armed-bandit example.

knowledge_points.description: A selection rule that combines estimated reward with an uncertainty allowance, favoring actions whose estimated upper bound is high.
learning_objectives: Explain the reward-estimate and uncertainty terms in UCB.
Relate UCB to balanced action selection.
common_misconceptions: Treating UCB as greedy selection by average reward only.
Assuming an underexplored action has no value until it has the best observed reward.
mastery_criteria: Can explain why UCB may select an uncertain action.

knowledge_points.description: A course-unit topic on Monte Carlo Tree Search and its role in the search summary material.
learning_objectives: Recognize Monte Carlo Tree Search as a course topic.
Locate the corresponding course-material source for a question.
common_misconceptions: Assuming Monte Carlo Tree Search is identical to breadth-first search.
Using an unverified source image as a factual explanation.
mastery_criteria: Can identify when a question concerns Monte Carlo Tree Search.
